faqs.q: How is the price for a Morristown wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. A Morristown colonial with squirrels at one dormer and a Speedwell-side Victorian with a raccoon litter and a fouled attic are separated by several lines of work, and the quote shows every one of them before a decision is asked. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Morristown ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. The morning running in Morristown usually traces to the shaded side of the house, where the canopy is thickest and the oldest eave boards are softest. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

Morristown.wildlife_intro:
Morristown is Morris County's historic seat: the Green and its 18th-century streets, Victorian and colonial neighborhoods climbing the hills, Speedwell Lake at the north end, and Jockey Hollow's woods just outside town. The housing is old, substantial, and complicated, with two centuries of additions. Squirrels and raccoons work the big attics and chimneys, bats hold colonies in the older homes near the Whippany River and the lake, groundhogs dig the hillside lots, and the town's heavy canopy bridges to rooflines on street after street. Suburban Morris Township wraps the whole town in more of the same.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Morristown's canopy is historic and protected in spirit, so the limb work here is surgical, the minimum cut that breaks the bridge, agreed with the owner before the saw comes out.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Parsippany-Troy Hills garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. Around the lakes the gardens sit downhill from wooded banks, and the groundhog's burrow in the bank is a short, covered commute from the beds; the bank is where the set goes. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Parsippany-Troy Hills porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Lake-community porches sit low over damp, sandy ground, and Parsippany skunks treat them as standard housing; screening them in February prevents the spring discovery. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

Parsippany-Troy Hills.wildlife_intro:
Parsippany is Morris County's crossroads suburb: Lake Parsippany and Lake Hiawatha's older lake communities, postwar subdivisions, and office parks along Routes 46, 80, and 287. The lakes and the township's many wooded buffers keep wildlife threaded through the neighborhoods. Squirrels and raccoons are the daily entries at the colonials' soffits, groundhogs dig the lots backing onto woods and fields, skunks work the lake-community lawns, and bats settle into attics near the water. Canada geese own the lakefront lawns, a deterrence-and-permit conversation rather than a removal one.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Parsippany lots back onto office-park woods, lake edges, and buffers in every direction, so the yard survey here reads the lot line and the ground just past it as one system.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Randolph Township homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Randolph Township host summer colonies, and in Morris County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Randolph Township?
faqs.a: Randolph Township sits in northern New Jersey, suburban in the east and Highland and lake country in the west, and the habitat in between the houses — Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Dover basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Dover's older basements the signs concentrate near the old coal bins and the river-side wall, and the entry is usually a utility penetration sealed with material a rat regards as a snack. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Dover attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. Hillside Dover attics produce the night-noise calls, and droppings usually distinguish a raccoon's latrine corner from a flying squirrel colony in a single visit. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

Dover.wildlife_intro:
Dover is an old mining and mill town on the Rockaway River: dense, older housing climbing the hills from Blackwell Street, brick and frame singles and doubles, and a working downtown. The housing's age and density set the call log. Rats work the older basements and the blocks behind the downtown businesses, raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs, squirrels gnaw the eaves of the hillside homes, and bats hold the attics along the river. The woods are never far, the river runs through the middle, and the animals commute along both.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Dover's doubles and attached rows share more than walls; entries are mapped across the connected rooflines so a sealing job does not simply relocate the tenant one house over.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Madison attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night-only scratching in Morris County often means bats, flying squirrels or raccoons, while daytime running usually points to gray squirrels. Around Lake Hopatcong, the cover close to housing means several species are plausible, so call us for an inspection and we will identify the animal before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Madison porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Madison with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: I found a snake in my Chatham Township yard — could it be venomous?
faqs.a: Possibly, in this part of New Jersey, which is why identification comes before everything. The northern copperhead (state-Threatened) favors rocky, wooded slopes here, and the timber rattlesnake (state-Endangered) holds on along the ridges; both are left strictly alone and referred to NJ Fish & Wildlife's Venomous Snake Response Team. The swamp edge produces mostly harmless water and garter snakes, but the township's rocky upland woods are within the copperhead's Morris County range, so a banded snake here is identified, not assumed. Most calls turn out to be harmless black rat snakes or garter snakes, which we can catch and release outdoors within 200 meters, as state policy allows.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Chatham Township attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. Swamp-edge attics are prime maternity roosts, and a June discovery in the township means the living-space seals go in immediately and the exclusion is dated for the August window. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

Chatham Township.wildlife_intro:
Chatham Township wraps around the Great Swamp's southern edge: affluent subdivisions of colonials on wooded lots, older homes along the swamp roads, and the Loantaka Brook corridor threading through. The swamp is one of New Jersey's great wildlife reservoirs, and the houses along it get the overflow. Squirrels and raccoons are constant at the rooflines, bats summer in the attics near the wetlands, groundhogs and skunks work the big lawns, and nonvenomous snakes slide out of the swamp edge into foundation plantings, with copperheads possible in the township's rockier woods.

The quiet months are the test. Anyone can empty an attic; keeping it empty through the next breeding season is the work. We leave each house with its entries mapped — what was sealed, with what material, and what to watch — and we flag the two or three weak points most likely to fail next, whether that is aging flashing, a settling addition, or a tree that will reach the roof in two more summers. Homeowners who walk that list each fall, the way they service a furnace, rarely meet us twice for the same animal. Chatham Township homes next to the swamp are never finished, only maintained, and the entry map we leave is written as a fall checklist for a property under year-round pressure.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Rockaway Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Morris County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in Rockaway Township?
faqs.a: Spring denning and the fall push indoors are the two busy waves in Morris County, with bat colonies and mole damage peaking in summer. If you are hearing noise or seeing digging in Rockaway Township, calling at the first sign almost always makes for a simpler, cheaper job.
